title: PS-20 Investigating potential relationships among key selection metrics of feed efficiency, pulmonary arterial pressure, and fertility metrics in beef bulls at high elevation
content:
Abstract
It is well established that reproductive and feed efficiency of the bull greatly impact the economic viability of cow-calf operations. Another key factor influencing economic viability in the Mountain West, is mortality of calves due to high altitude disease. The objective of this study is to evaluate the relationship between pulmonary arterial pressure (PAP), reproductive soundness and performance in bulls at high altitude. Beef bulls of various breeds were consigned to the 2024 University of Wyoming High Altitude Bull Test and Sale (n = 35) and managed at 2190 meters elevation for 146 days. Feed efficiency was monitored for 81 days in the Vytelle SENSE™ system with weights collected every 2 weeks allowing for the calculation of dry matter intake (DMI), average daily gain (ADG), residual feed intake (RFI), feed conversion ratio (FCR), and weight per day of age (WPDA). These metrics were utilized to create a selection index that included ADG, RFI, and WPDA. Pulmonary arterial pressure was measured at d 44 and d 106 and was utilized to assign risk for heart failure (low risk < 42 mmHg; moderate risk 42-49 mmHg; high risk > 49 mmHg). On d 117, a breeding soundness exam was conducted by a veterinarian. These data were analyzed in SAS v9.04 where associations between fertility metrics, PAP, and performance metrics were determined using PROC CORR. Feed efficiency metrics and PAP data were analyzed using PROC GLIMMIX with fixed effects of initial BSE conclusion (n = 24 pass; n = 9 fail) and initial (low, n = 15; moderate, n = 9; high = 9) and final PAP risk (low, n = 19; moderate = 4; high, n = 10). Scrotal circumference tended (r = -0.03; P = 0.08) to be negatively correlated with diastolic pressure and was positively correlated (r ≥ 0.35; P ≤ 0.04) with final weight, DMI, ADG, WPDA, and index. Motility tended (r = 0.30; P = 0.09) to be positively correlated with WPDA and was positively correlated (r = 0.71; P ≤ 0.0001). Morphology tended (r = 0.30; P = 0.09) to be positively correlated with DMI and RFI (r = 0.31; P = 0.08). Initial and final PAP did not differ (P ≥ 0.66) by BSE outcome. There were no differences (P ≥ 0.15) in ADG, FCR, RFI, WPDA or index for BSE outcome, initial or final risk. These data highlight a potential relationship between feed efficiency, PAP risk, and reproductive efficiency in beef bulls. Further work is warranted to evaluate the potential indirect responses in bull selection with traits that largely influence economic viability of cow-calf operations.
